## 1. Setup & Data Loading

We use `tidymodels` to structure a reproducible machine learning pipeline and prevent data leakage between training and testing sets.

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(sf)
library(here)
library(ranger)      # Fast Random Forest engine
library(glmnet)      # Regularized linear regression (Ridge/Lasso)
library(finetune)    # Speeds up model tuning
#install.packages("vip", repos = c("https://bgreenwell.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
library(vip)

# Load your dataset (update the file path/format as needed)
tracts_raw <- st_read(here("data/gee_lstdata/lab6_gee_lstdata.gpkg")) %>%
  st_set_geometry(NULL)

# Parse State FIPS from GISJOIN (characters 2-3 in NHGIS format, e.g., "G060..." -> "06" = CA)
tracts <- tracts_raw %>%
  mutate(
    state_fips = str_sub(GISJOIN, 2, 3),
    county_fips = str_sub(GISJOIN, 2, 6),
    state = case_when(
      state_fips == "06" ~ "CA",
      state_fips == "41" ~ "OR",
      state_fips == "53" ~ "WA",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    # Treat land cover codes and binary flags as factors
    nlcd_class = as.factor(nlcd_class)
  ) %>%
  # Remove rows with missing target values
  drop_na(tree_cover_pct)

glimpse(tracts)
```

## 2. Data Splitting (Spatial Holdout)

Because census tracts exhibit strong spatial autocorrelation, a standard random split would place adjacent tracts in both the training and test sets, artificially inflating accuracy. 

Here, we use a **group-aware split** (`group_initial_split`) so entire counties are kept intact in either training or testing. Below, we parse County FIPS from `GISJOIN` (`str_sub(GISJOIN, 2, 6)`).

```{r split}
set.seed(4300)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(county_fips = str_sub(GISJOIN, 2, 6))

# Hold out 20% of counties completely from training
tract_split <- group_initial_split(tracts, group = county_fips, prop = 0.80)

train_data <- training(tract_split)
test_data  <- testing(tract_split)

cat("Training tracts:", nrow(train_data), "| Test tracts:", nrow(test_data), "\n")
```

## 3. Preprocessing & Feature Engineering (`recipes`)

All preprocessing steps are defined in a `recipe` and estimated **strictly on `train_data`**. 

* Note: We exclude `GISJOIN`, `nlcd_label` (redundant with `nlcd_class`), and spatial ID columns from being used as predictors (`update_role(..., new_role = "id")`).

```{r recipe}
canopy_recipe <- recipe(tree_cover_pct ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
  # Mark identifiers so they are retained for mapping/diagnostics but not modeled
  update_role("GISJOIN", "gisjn_tct", "GEOID", "STATEFP", "COUNTYFP", "TRACTCE","n_bg",
      "county_fips", "nlcd_label","state","state_fips",
      new_role = "id") %>%
  # Handle any missing predictor values using training set medians/modes
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  # Collapse rare NLCD classes (if any exist in <1% of tracts) to prevent dummy mismatch
  step_other(nlcd_class, threshold = 0.01) %>%
  # One-hot encode categorical variables
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) %>%
  # Remove zero-variance predictors
  step_zv(all_predictors()) %>%
  # Normalize numeric predictors (required for Ridge/Lasso; harmless for Random Forest)
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

canopy_recipe
```

## 4. Define Candidate Models & Resampling

Before touching our held-out test set—which acts as a final, one-time exam—we need a way to tune model settings and compare algorithms using only the training data. We do this with **5-fold cross-validation (`group_vfold_cv`)**:

* **How folds work:** Our training data is divided into 5 roughly equal chunks ("folds"). In Round 1, the model trains on Folds 2–5 (80% of the training set) and predicts on Fold 1 (the remaining 20%, acting as a temporary validation set). This repeats five times until every fold has served once as the validation set, and the resulting error scores (RMSE, MAE, $R^2$) are averaged together.
* **Why we group by county:** Because adjacent census tracts share similar climate and land cover characteristics, standard random folds would leak spatial information across the training/validation boundary. Grouping by `county_fips` forces the model to predict tree canopy in entirely unseen counties during every round.

We compare two candidate models across these folds:
1. **Elastic Net Regression (`glmnet`):** A regularized linear baseline that shrinks coefficients to handle strongly correlated remote-sensing indices (`ndvi`, `ndbi`, `ndwi`, `lst_c`).
2. **Random Forest (`ranger`):** A non-linear ensemble of decision trees capable of capturing complex interactions (such as how elevation and precipitation jointly shape forest cover across coastal vs. inland regions).

```{r models}
# 1. Baseline: Regularized Linear Regression (tuned penalty & mixture)
enet_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

# 2. Candidate: Random Forest (tuned mtry and min_n)
rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = 200) %>%
  set_engine("ranger") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

# Spatial/Group 5-fold cross-validation on the training set (grouped by county)
set.seed(4300)
cv_folds <- group_vfold_cv(train_data, group = county_fips, v = 5)
```

## 5. Hyperparameter Tuning via Cross-Validation

We use `workflow_set()` to tune and evaluate both models across the exact same cross-validation folds.

Unlike standard regression coefficients—which the algorithm learns directly from the data—**hyperparameters** are structural settings for the model we have to choose *before* training begins. Think of it like cooking: parameters are the exact internal temperatures and chemical changes happening inside the oven, while hyperparameters are the dials you set on the outside—oven temperature, rack position, and baking time.

Because we cannot know the ideal settings ahead of time, `tune_grid()` uses **grid search**:

* **Testing candidate combinations (`grid = 10`):** `tidymodels` automatically generates 10 distinct, space-filling combinations of hyperparameter values for each model. It trains and evaluates every combination across all 5 cross-validation folds ($10 \text{ combinations} \times 5 \text{ folds} = 50 \text{ model fits per algorithm}$) to see which settings produce the lowest prediction error.
* **Balancing speed vs. precision:** A small grid of 10 keeps computation fast while still exploring a broad range of model behavior—ideal for exploratory analysis or classroom demonstrations. In a final production workflow, increasing this grid (e.g., `grid = 25` or `30`) searches the parameter space more finely to squeeze out incremental gains in accuracy.


We also save the resulting tuned model to an rds file since it takes awhile to run.

```{r tune}
wf_set <- workflow_set(
  preproc = list(base = canopy_recipe),
  models  = list(elastic_net = enet_spec, random_forest = rf_spec)
)

# Tune across a small grid (increase grid size for production runs)
# WARNING: this takes a few minutes
tune_file <- here("data/gee_lstdata/lstdata_tune_results.rds")

# Delete the old cached file once (or comment out unlink() after running)
if (file.exists(tune_file)) file.remove(tune_file)

if (!file.exists(tune_file)) {
  tune_results <- wf_set %>%
    workflow_map(
      fn        = "tune_race_anova",
      resamples = cv_folds,
      grid      = 10,
      metrics   = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq),
      seed      = 4300
    )
  write_rds(tune_results, tune_file)
} else {
  tune_results <- read_rds(tune_file)
}

# Compare cross-validated performance
collect_metrics(tune_results) %>%
  filter(.metric %in% c("rmse", "rsq")) %>%
  group_by(wflow_id, .metric) %>%
  slice_min(mean, n = 1) %>%
  select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err)
```



## 6. Finalize & Evaluate on the Held-Out Test Set

We extract the best Random Forest configuration, fit it to the full training set, and evaluate it once on the untouched `test_data` using `last_fit()`.

```{r evaluate}
best_rf_params <- tune_results %>%
  extract_workflow_set_result("base_random_forest") %>%
  select_best(metric = "rmse")

final_rf_wf <- tune_results %>%
  extract_workflow("base_random_forest") %>%
  finalize_workflow(best_rf_params)

# Only compute variable importance on the final winning model
final_rf_wf <- final_rf_wf %>%
  update_model(
    rand_forest(
      mtry  = best_rf_params$mtry,
      min_n = best_rf_params$min_n,
      trees = 500
    ) %>%
      set_engine("ranger", importance = "permutation") %>%
      set_mode("regression")
  )

# Fit on all training data and evaluate on held-out test counties
final_fit <- last_fit(final_rf_wf, split = tract_split, metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq))

# Out-of-sample test metrics
collect_metrics(final_fit)
```

## 7. Diagnostics & Variable Importance

Finally, we inspect which physical variables drive predictions and plot predicted vs. observed canopy cover across states to check for systematic regional bias.

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-width: 8

# 1. Permutation Variable Importance
final_fit %>%
  extract_fit_parsnip() %>%
  vip(num_features = 12, aesthetics = list(fill = "#2c7fb8")) +
  labs(
    title = "Top Predictors of Census Tract Tree Canopy Cover",
    subtitle = "Permutation importance from tuned Random Forest"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# 2. Predicted vs. Observed Scatterplot by State
test_predictions <- collect_predictions(final_fit) %>%
  bind_cols(test_data %>% select(GISJOIN, state, county_fips))

# Calculate state-level R2 (and RMSE if helpful) for facet annotations
state_metrics <- test_predictions %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  summarize(
    rsq  = rsq_vec(truth = tree_cover_pct, estimate = .pred),
    rmse = rmse_vec(truth = tree_cover_pct, estimate = .pred),
    label = sprintf("R² = %.2f\nRMSE = %.1f%%", rsq, rmse),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot with R2 annotated in the top-left corner of each facet
ggplot(test_predictions, aes(x = tree_cover_pct, y = .pred, color = state)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_text(
    data = state_metrics,
    aes(x = 5, y = 95, label = label),
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = 1,
    size = 3.5,
    color = "black",
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ state) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Out-of-Sample Predictions vs. Observed MODIS Tree Cover (%)",
    x = "Observed Tree Cover (%)",
    y = "Predicted Tree Cover (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
